On August 26, 2026, a deadly flash flood struck the Himalayas along the border of Nepal and Tibet, causing devastating loss of life and wiping out vital infrastructure. While initial reports blamed an earthquake or a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF), satellite analysis revealed a far more terrifying reality: a massive 600-meter glacier block detached and fell 1,200 meters straight down. In this full-length documentary, we break down the physics, geography, and political failures behind the disaster. The friction of millions of tons of rock and ice falling at highway speeds pulverized the glacier into water in mid-air, creating a temporary debris dam in the Lhende Khola river. More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday’s catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth’s temperature rose due to human activities such as burning oil, gas, and coal, the likelihood of such disasters increased, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which were warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world. #Himalayan #Flood #Nepal #Share #FY
